messages.content: Before we get into the build, where will this system run? Hosting shapes the architecture, the running cost, and the compliance defaults, so it's worth settling early. If you're not sure yet, pick "Nothing yet" and we'll leave it open.
Thanks, cloud account noted. Next, since you're on a cloud account, the team's experience with that platform shapes which services we'd recommend. Which cloud provider do you use today?

I use Azure; we’re already fully integrated with Azure Active Directory for single sign-on across all hospital systems, and our current infrastructure—HL7 interfaces, FHIR APIs, and internal microservices—runs on Azure. That means we’ll build this new tool using Azure App Services, Azure SQL Database, and leverage Azure AD B2C for any potential external access, keeping identity management consistent.

Azure with Azure AD for sign-on is a clear fit, and I'll note it as the cloud platform. Which existing systems must this tool work with? Knowing this matters because each system shapes the data we pull and push and how much integration work the build takes. If nothing else needs connecting, say "none" and we'll move on.

The tool must integrate with two systems: our existing Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system, Epic, via its FHIR API (version STU3), and our ward-level nurse scheduling and shift management system, which uses a REST API hosted on Azure. The FHIR API will provide patient demographics and current admission status, and the nurse shift system will provide real-time ward staffing data to validate who’s authorized to enter notes. We’ll use Azure API Management to proxy and secure these integrations, ensuring compliance with HIPAA and our hospital’s data governance policies.

Thanks for the integration detail. Two systems to connect: Epic via FHIR STU3, and the ward shift system via REST, both proxied through Azure API Management. I'll record both.

Next, who will build this? It shapes how the specification and plan are phrased. If you're unsure, we'll assume a coding agent.

I’ll be leading the build with a small team: two full-stack developers, one frontend specialist (React), and one DevOps engineer. We’re using Azure DevOps for CI/CD pipelines, with infrastructure-as-code via Terraform, and we’ll follow our hospital’s secure coding standards, including static analysis with SonarQube and dependency scanning with Snyk.

Thanks for the team detail. Since you're building it with an in-house team, I'll record that and skip the builder question. Next, what problem does this solve, and for whom? Right now nurses type each note twice, once into the patient system and once into a spreadsheet, and we need to know who feels that pain most and what happens if it stays unsolved.

The primary users are ward nurses, specifically those on medical-surgical and intensive care units who manage 12–15 patients per shift. They currently enter the same clinical note—like vital signs, medication changes, or patient behavior—into Epic’s FHIR-compliant note field and into a shared Excel-based ward log used by the charge nurse and clinical leads. This duplication causes delays (averaging 3–5 minutes per patient per shift), increases documentation errors by ~18% according to our last audit, and creates a compliance risk when notes don’t align across systems. If left unsolved, it leads to nurse burnout, inconsistent handoffs, and audit failures during regulatory reviews.

That's a clear picture of the problem, with real numbers behind it. Before we pick any frameworks, what does your team know best? A stack the team already knows usually beats a slightly better one nobody has used, so this shapes our recommendations. If you're not sure, we'll record it as unknown.

Noted: the team works in .NET and C#. That fits well with Azure App Services and Azure SQL, so I'll record it as the team's stack.

Next, who uses this tool day to day? Please name the roles and what each one needs to do first, starting with the ward nurse, since they're the main users we've described.

The primary user is the ward nurse, who needs to log in via Azure AD SSO, select a patient from their assigned shift roster (pulled from the ward scheduling API), and enter a free-text clinical note using a clean, mobile-responsive form that auto-saves every 30 seconds. The secondary user is the charge nurse, who needs to view a real-time dashboard of all entered notes per ward, filter by patient or nurse, and export a summary to PDF for shift handoff. The tertiary user is the clinical informatics lead, who occasionally audits note distribution and duplication rates via a secure admin portal with role-based access control.

Thanks, those three roles give us a clear shape. Next, when does version one need to be in use? The date decides how much we can cut from the first release. If there's no fixed date, we'll plan without one.

We need version one live by October 15, 2024, to align with the hospital’s annual compliance audit cycle and our scheduled EMR system upgrade in early November. That gives us 12 weeks from today to deliver a minimum viable product with core note entry, FHIR push to Epic, and basic dashboard visibility for charge nurses—no advanced analytics or export formats beyond PDF in v1.

Thanks, the October 15 deadline is recorded, and it fits the audit cycle and the early-November EMR upgrade. Version one covers note entry, the FHIR push to Epic, and a basic charge nurse dashboard, with PDF as the only export.

Next, who else touches this tool? Besides ward nurses, charge nurses and the informatics lead, does anyone else need access, such as a pharmacist or a hospital IT administrator?

Yes, hospital IT administrators need access to the tool’s health monitoring dashboard—available via Azure Monitor and Application Insights—to track API latency, error rates, and authentication failures. They’ll use it to detect issues before nurses report them, especially during high-traffic shift changes. Additionally, a pharmacy liaison may need read-only access to the note feed for specific alerts (e.g., “patient refusing medication”) to initiate interventions, but only with explicit approval and audit logging. All access is governed by Azure AD roles and requires MFA.

Thanks for the IT administrator and pharmacy liaison details. Next, is there a budget range for this build? It affects whether we lean toward building or buying parts of the solution. If you're not sure, we'll leave it undecided.

We have a budget of $85,000 for the full build and deployment of version one, covering dev time, Azure infrastructure, API management, and compliance testing. This allows us to build the core features in-house using our .NET stack and Azure services, but we’ll use a commercial FHIR client library (Hl7.FhirNetCore) to reduce integration effort and avoid re-inventing the HL7 standard. We won’t buy a full off-the-shelf solution, but we’ll license secure logging and monitoring tools from Azure Marketplace within this budget.

Thanks, the $85,000 budget is recorded. It covers in-house development on the .NET and Azure stack, the commercial FHIR client library, and licensed logging and monitoring tools.

Next, the product itself: what must the ward nurse be able to do on the first screen after signing in? Describe the action in your own words, for example entering a note for a patient on their roster.

After signing in, the ward nurse sees a clean, responsive dashboard that lists all patients on their current shift, pulled from the ward scheduling API in real time. The first action is to click a patient card, which opens a pre-filled note form with that patient’s name, MRN, bed number, and admission date—auto-populated from the FHIR API. The nurse then types a free-text clinical note (with auto-save every 30 seconds), selects a note type from a predefined dropdown (e.g., “Vital Signs,” “Medication Change,” “Behavioral Concern”), and clicks “Submit.” On submission, the note is immediately sent to Epic via the FHIR API and appears in the ward log dashboard for charge nurses to review.

That workflow is clear, and I'll capture it as the core nurse flow. One sizing question: roughly how many users will use this at launch? It decides how much capacity we plan for and the hosting defaults. If you're unsure, we'll assume under 100.

We expect about 160 active ward nurses across the three medical-surgical and ICU units to use the tool at launch, mostly during two 12-hour shifts per day. This means we’ll design for peak concurrency of 60–80 users simultaneously entering or editing notes, with an expected average of 120 concurrent sessions during shift change hours (7–9 AM and 7–9 PM). We’ll provision Azure App Service with 4 vCPUs and scale up to 8 instances during peak times, using Azure autoscale rules based on CPU and request queue length.

Thanks, that answers the sizing question. About 160 nurses, with peaks near 120 concurrent sessions at shift change, means the hosting plan has to handle far more than the under-100 default I was prepared to assume. I'll record it as your figure.

Next, what happens to a note if Epic is unreachable when the nurse clicks Submit? Should it be held and retried automatically, or should the nurse be blocked until it goes through?

If Epic is unreachable during submission, the note is immediately persisted to our Azure SQL Database with a status of “Pending” and a retry queue is triggered via Azure Service Bus. The system automatically retries the FHIR POST every 30 seconds for up to 15 minutes, with exponential backoff. If it fails after 15 minutes, the nurse receives a notification in-app: “Note saved locally—sync failed. Contact IT if issue persists.” The charge nurse dashboard also flags pending notes by red icon, and the IT admin sees retry failures in Azure Monitor. This ensures no data loss and keeps nurses productive during transient outages.

Thanks for the retry design. It covers Epic outages without losing notes.

Next, which compliance regimes apply to this data? This changes hosting, access and audit requirements. This system will hold patient health information, so I'd default to HIPAA plus your hospital data governance policy. Should we keep that?

Yes, we’ll enforce HIPAA compliance and our hospital’s internal data governance policy, which includes mandatory encryption at rest and in transit (using Azure’s managed keys and TLS 1.3), audit logging for all access and modifications (retained for 7 years), and strict role-based access control via Azure AD. All FHIR data transfers are subject to our audit trail policy, and we’ll enable Microsoft Purview for data classification and discovery. We’ll also ensure that no data leaves the U.S. region (Azure East US) and that all backups are encrypted and stored in a separate region for disaster recovery.

Thanks, that covers the compliance picture: HIPAA, your hospital data governance policy, encryption at rest and in transit, seven-year audit logs, Azure AD role-based access, U.S.-only data residency, and an encrypted backup region for disaster recovery.

I'll record that as the compliance answer for this build, so we won't ask about it again.

Understood. All compliance requirements are documented and will guide the architecture, data flows, and access controls throughout the build. I’ll ensure the team reviews them in the design phase and includes them in the system’s security baseline.

Thanks, the compliance requirements are settled and will guide the design.

Next, let's confirm the roles. Besides the ward nurse, charge nurse, clinical informatics lead, IT administrator and pharmacy liaison, is there anyone else who will use or manage this tool?

No other roles require direct access at launch. The pharmacy liaison will only have read-only access through a curated view in the charge nurse dashboard, and no other departments—like respiratory therapy or social work—need to enter or manage notes. We’ve excluded those roles to keep the first release focused and aligned with the October 15 deadline. Any future expansion will require a new feature request and formal risk assessment.

Thanks for confirming the role list. One thing to pin down: the pharmacy liaison gets read-only access through a curated view in the charge nurse dashboard. Which notes should that view show, all notes for a unit, or only notes that carry an alert such as "patient refusing medication"?

Got it: the pharmacy liaison sees only alert-flagged notes. Can you walk me through one example? Take a note flagged as "patient refusing medication": what does the liaison see on screen, and what do they do next?

When a nurse submits a note with the alert type “Patient refusing medication,” the system tags it in Azure SQL with a `priority_flag = true` and sets `alert_type = "refusal"`. The pharmacy liaison, viewing the curated dashboard, sees a red banner notification highlighting the note, with the patient’s name, MRN, bed number, time of note, and the full text: “Patient refuses IV antibiotics; stated ‘I don’t want to get sicker.’” They can click to open it, which triggers an automated workflow: a Microsoft Teams message is sent to the pharmacy team channel with a link to the note, and a ticket is created in our incident tracking system (ServiceNow) with priority level 2. The liaison does not edit or delete the note—only reviews and escalates.

The example makes the liaison's role clear: read-only review, with a Teams message and a ServiceNow ticket as the escalation path. One gap remains. Who is allowed to open an alert-flagged note, and does each open need a reason from the liaison that gets audit-logged?

Only the pharmacy liaison and the charge nurse can open an alert-flagged note, and each access is logged in Azure Monitor with the user ID, timestamp, IP address, and the note’s MRN. When the liaison opens the note, they must select a reason from a dropdown—“Initiate intervention,” “Review for clinical risk,” or “Confirm no action”—which is stored in the audit log and visible in the data governance portal. This ensures accountability and supports our 7-year audit retention policy. No other role may access alert notes directly.

Thanks, the audit trail for alert-flagged notes is clear: only the liaison and charge nurse can open them, each open needs a reason, and every access is logged.

Next, let's turn these workflows into user stories. Starting with the ward nurse: when they finish a shift, what should they be able to check before leaving, such as whether any notes are still pending?

At the end of their shift, the ward nurse can access a “Shift Summary” view that shows all notes they submitted during the shift, with color-coded status: green for “Synced to Epic,” yellow for “Pending retry,” and red for “Failed after 15 minutes.” They can tap any failed note to see the error message and retry it manually if desired. The system also highlights any notes they flagged as “urgent” or “alert” so they can confirm handoffs were properly escalated. This summary is auto-saved and available in the app for 24 hours after shift end, and can be exported to PDF for personal records.

Thanks for the shift summary. Before we go further, I need to raise a gap in the Epic integration. It is named as FHIR STU3 for demographics and admission status, but we have not defined the contract: endpoint, payload shape, authentication, and error responses.

Default: we record the contract as FHIR STU3 with OAuth 2.0 client credentials through Azure API Management, and map each error to the retry rules you described. That means the developers will have a defined interface to build against before any integration work starts.

Do you want to keep that default, or do you have a specific Epic endpoint and auth method to use instead?

Thanks, the Epic contract default is accepted: FHIR STU3 with OAuth 2.0 client credentials through Azure API Management, with errors mapped to your retry rules.

Back to the stories. For the charge nurse, what is the first thing they do when they open their dashboard at the start of a shift?

At the start of their shift, the charge nurse opens the dashboard and sees a real-time summary of all ward notes from the prior shift: a list of patients with active notes, color-coded by status—green for “synced,” yellow for “pending,” and red for “failed.” They immediately see any alert-flagged notes (e.g., “refusing medication”) in a dedicated section at the top with a red badge, and a count of unresolved issues. They can click “View Full Log” to drill into the full note history per patient or export the overview to PDF for handoff. The system auto-refreshes every 2 minutes during the shift.

Thanks, the charge nurse's start-of-shift view is clear: alert-flagged notes at the top, status colors, and a two-minute refresh.

Next, the charge nurse can export the overview to PDF for handoff. Who is the recipient of that handoff, and does the export need to be logged like alert-note access?

The PDF handoff is shared with the incoming charge nurse and the unit manager, who receive it via secure email through Azure Logic Apps, with encryption and a 7-day expiration link. The export is logged in the audit trail with the user ID, timestamp, patient count, and recipient email, and stored in Azure Blob Storage with a 7-year retention policy—exactly like alert-note access. This ensures compliance with HIPAA and our internal data governance policy, and allows us to trace any data sharing during audits.

Thanks, the PDF handoff is now clear: it goes to the incoming charge nurse and unit manager by encrypted email with a seven-day link, and every export is audit-logged.

Let's go one level deeper on the ward nurse. When a nurse submits a note and Epic is down, what do they see on screen while the note waits to retry, and when does the system notify them?

While waiting to retry, the nurse sees a persistent notification at the top of the screen: “Your note is pending sync—will retry automatically. Status: Retry attempt #2 (30 seconds ago).” The retry status updates every 30 seconds with a progress graphic. If the note fails after 15 minutes, the system triggers a push notification (via Azure Notification Hub) and displays a modal: “Note saved locally—sync failed due to Epic outage. Contact IT if issue persists.” The message remains visible until acknowledged, ensuring no note is silently lost—this is logged as a failed write event in Azure Monitor, visible to the IT team.

The retry experience is clear, and it gives us a concrete requirement to capture. Let's start the functional requirements with the most basic capability: when a nurse opens the app, what must they be able to do first, before any note is written?

When a nurse opens the app, they must be able to authenticate via Azure AD SSO and immediately see their assigned shift roster—displayed as a list of patient cards—with real-time status indicators (e.g., “Active,” “Discharged,” “Transfer”). Each card shows the patient’s name, MRN, bed number, and current admission status, pulled from the FHIR API. This data must load within 3 seconds, and the nurse must be able to click any patient card to begin note entry—even if the network is slow, with all patient data cached locally for up to 5 minutes.

Thanks, the roster requirement is recorded: Azure AD sign-in, a patient-card roster loading within three seconds, and five-minute local caching.

I also need to flag a gap. The ward shift system is named as a real-time staffing source, but we have no contract for it yet: no endpoint, payload shape, authentication method, or error format.

Default: REST on Azure behind Azure API Management, with OAuth 2.0 client credentials and the same error-mapping approach as Epic. That means the roster and staffing data follow one integration pattern.

Do you accept this default for the ward shift system?
(I picked: {"type":"yes_no","value":true})

Thanks, the ward shift system default is accepted: REST on Azure behind API Management, with OAuth 2.0 client credentials and the same error mapping as Epic.

Staying on functional requirements: when a nurse opens the roster, the cards show admission status. If a patient is marked "Transfer" in Epic but the ward shift system shows the bed as empty, which status should the nurse see, and should the card warn them?

The nurse sees the status from the ward shift system—the bed is empty—so the card shows “Bed Empty” and is dimmed, with a small tooltip: “Patient transferred per ward system; note may not be relevant.” The card does not display the Epic admission status of “Transfer” in this case, because the shift system’s real-time bed state takes precedence. If the nurse attempts to enter a note for that patient, a modal appears: “Patient not assigned to this ward—note will not sync to Epic. Confirm continue?” This prevents invalid data entry and maintains data integrity.

The bed-state precedence is clear. Next, the modal says a note "will not sync to Epic" if the patient isn't on the ward. Should the nurse be able to confirm and save the note locally anyway, or should the entry be blocked entirely?

"Yes" is ambiguous here: it could mean the nurse can confirm and save locally, or that entry should be blocked. Please tell me which: should the nurse be able to save the note locally, knowing it will not reach Epic?

Yes, the nurse can confirm and save the note locally—this is allowed only if the patient is marked as “Transferred” or “Discharged” in the ward shift system, and the note is tagged with a `local_only` flag. The system saves it to Azure SQL with status “Local Save” and includes a warning in the audit log: “Note saved locally—patient not on active ward.” The charge nurse dashboard shows a count of such notes, and they are purged after 7 days unless manually reviewed. This balances clinical need with data integrity and compliance.

Thanks, local-only saves are clear: allowed only for transferred or discharged patients, tagged `local_only`, audit-logged, and purged after seven days unless reviewed.

Let's move to business rules. Which of these notes can a ward nurse submit to Epic: only notes for patients currently assigned to their own ward, or notes for patients on any ward they are covering?

Got it: nurses can submit to Epic only for patients on their own ward. A nurse covering another ward will not be able to send notes for those patients.

Next, a related case: a nurse on their own ward has a patient marked Transferred in the shift system, and they try to submit a note to Epic instead of saving it locally. Should the system block that submission, or allow it to sync since Epic may still show the patient on this ward?

The system should allow the submission to sync to Epic even if the ward shift system shows “Transferred,” but only if the note is tagged with a `transferred_patient` flag and includes a warning in the audit log: “Note submitted for transferred patient—Epic may reflect outdated status.” This is because Epic may still show the patient as admitted for up to 30 minutes after the transfer, and blocking the sync would force nurses to wait or use local save, which increases fragmentation. The charge nurse dashboard flags such notes for review, and IT can correlate discrepancies between systems during audits.

Thanks, the transferred-patient submission rule is clear: sync to Epic is allowed, the note is tagged `transferred_patient`, an audit warning is written, and the charge nurse dashboard flags it.

One thing to confirm: a note can be a "local save" for a transferred patient, or a "submit with transferred flag." Both apply to the same patient status, so the nurse's choice decides which path the note takes. Does the nurse choose between saving locally and submitting, or does the system choose automatically based on the Epic status?

Thanks, so the nurse decides each time. Let's close the gap on the local-save side: local notes are purged after seven days unless reviewed. Who is allowed to review a local-only note, and what does review do: release it to Epic, or simply mark it as reviewed and keep it?

Only the charge nurse or the clinical informatics lead can review a local-only note. When they open it, they see the full content and a status of “Local Save – Awaiting Review.” They can either: (1) click “Review and Release” to re-submit the note to Epic, with a new `released_local` timestamp and full audit trail, or (2) click “Mark as Reviewed – Keep Local” to confirm they’ve seen it and prevent it from being purged. If not reviewed within 7 days, the note is automatically purged from Azure SQL and moved to a secure archive in Azure Blob Storage for audit retrieval, but not accessible in the app.

Thanks, the review rules for local-only notes are recorded: charge nurse or informatics lead can release to Epic or keep local, and unreviewed notes are archived after seven days.

Now let's move to acceptance criteria, starting with the simplest check. When a ward nurse signs in, how would we confirm the roster is working correctly: should we verify that only patients assigned to that nurse's ward appear, or that the cards load within three seconds?

We’ll confirm the roster is working correctly by verifying two things: first, that only patients assigned to the nurse’s current ward (per the ward shift system) appear in the list, and second, that the roster loads within 3 seconds on a standard hospital tablet (Android 12, 4GB RAM) over the hospital Wi-Fi network. We’ll use Azure Application Insights to measure load time, and the frontend will log a `roster_load_time` metric. If either check fails—any patient outside the ward appears, or load time exceeds 3 seconds—the test fails.

That's a testable roster check. Before we write it up, one detail: when the ward shift system and Epic disagree, which one decides whether a patient counts as "on the ward" for this test? Per the bed-state rule, we've been treating the ward shift system as authoritative.

Yes, the ward shift system’s real-time bed assignment is authoritative for determining whether a patient appears in the nurse’s roster. If the shift system shows a bed as unassigned or the patient as transferred, they do not appear—even if Epic still lists the patient as admitted. This ensures the roster reflects current staffing reality, not outdated EMR state. The discrepancy is logged in the audit trail with timestamps from both systems, and flagged in the charge nurse dashboard if the patient was recently transferred.

Thanks, the ward shift system is confirmed as authoritative for the roster, and Epic-only admissions stay hidden.

Next, let's make the acceptance criteria concrete for the transfer case. Suppose a patient is transferred off the ward at 2:00 PM, Epic still shows them admitted, and the ward shift system updates at 2:01 PM. Should the test require the roster to drop that patient within a set time after the shift system updates, and if so, how many seconds?

Yes, the test must verify that the roster drops the patient within 60 seconds of the ward shift system updating their status—specifically, the system must detect the change via the REST API polling interval (set to 30 seconds) and refresh the roster within 90 seconds of the update. We’ll measure this with a test that simulates a shift system update at t=0 and checks for the absence of the patient card at t=60 seconds. If the patient remains visible beyond 90 seconds, the test fails. This ensures real-time alignment with staffing changes while accounting for network latency and polling cycles.

The 90-second ceiling is clear. Your test checks absence at 60 seconds but fails only after 90, so a card still visible at 61 seconds would pass. Which should it be: the card must be gone by 60 seconds, or the 90-second limit is the only pass condition?

Thanks, the pass condition is now set: the patient card must be gone within 90 seconds of the shift system update, with the 60-second check removed.

Let's move to the technical side. You've already chosen .NET and C#, so the next decision is the frontend. Do you want to use React, given that your team has a React specialist?

Yes, we’ll use React for the frontend—specifically, Create React App with TypeScript, leveraging Material UI for consistent styling and accessibility compliance (WCAG 2.1 AA). The React app will run in a container on Azure App Service, with a Content Security Policy (CSP) and strict XSS protections enabled, and all static assets served over HTTPS. We’ll use React Router for navigation, and the app will be built with PWA support for offline note entry during network failures.

React with TypeScript is recorded. Your answer also includes Create React App, Material UI, React Router and PWA offline support, which are several separate decisions, so let's take them one at a time.

Offline note entry is the one with the biggest build impact. Should version one support creating and editing notes while the device has no network connection, or should it only queue notes after a submission fails?

"Yes" could mean full offline note creation and editing, or only queuing a note after a failed submission. Those lead to very different builds: full offline editing needs local storage, conflict handling and a service worker, while queuing only needs the retry path we've already defined. Which one do you mean?

Yes, version one must support full offline note creation and editing—nurses must be able to start typing a note, save it locally, and edit it later even if the device loses network connectivity. The app uses IndexedDB for local persistence, a service worker to cache assets and handle offline state, and a conflict resolution strategy that prioritizes the latest version based on timestamp when sync succeeds. If a nurse edits a note offline and another version exists in Epic, the system logs a conflict and prompts the charge nurse to resolve it via the dashboard. This ensures no data loss and supports the 30-second auto-save requirement even without network.

Offline full editing is recorded, along with IndexedDB, a service worker, and timestamp-based conflict handling.

One gap to close before we finish security. Your access rules name roles like ward nurse, charge nurse, pharmacy liaison and informatics lead, but the Azure AD roles that enforce them aren't defined yet. Default: one Azure AD app role per user role (WardNurse, ChargeNurse, PharmacyLiaison, ClinicalInformaticsLead, HospitalITAdministrator), assigned through Azure AD groups. That means access is granted by group membership and revoked when someone leaves a ward. Keep this default?

Thanks, the Azure AD role mapping is confirmed: one app role per user role, granted through Azure AD groups.

Staying with the technical area, the open decision is how the React app and the .NET backend talk to each other. Default: the React app calls a .NET Web API, which is the only component that calls Epic and the ward shift system through Azure API Management, so no tokens or Epic credentials reach the browser. That means the browser never holds FHIR credentials. Keep this default?

Yes, we’ll keep the default: the React app communicates with the .NET backend via HTTPS, and the backend—running as a secure Azure App Service with managed identity—calls Epic and the ward shift system through Azure API Management using client credentials. The frontend never receives or stores FHIR tokens or API keys; all authentication is handled server-side. The API endpoints use JWT bearer tokens issued by Azure AD, validated by the backend, and all data is encrypted in transit using TLS 1.3. This ensures no credential exposure in the browser and meets our compliance requirements.

Thanks, the backend-centred architecture is recorded: the browser never touches Epic credentials, and the .NET backend holds the calls to Epic and the ward shift system.

Now the data side. Which records does the app need to store in Azure SQL: patient notes, the shift roster, audit entries, or something else? Default: notes, the local-only queue, and audit events, with the roster read live from the ward shift system rather than stored.

Yes, we’ll store patient notes, the local-only note queue, and audit events in Azure SQL, but not the shift roster—its data is pulled live from the ward shift system every 30 seconds via the REST API. Notes and queued entries are stored with a `created_at`, `updated_at`, `patient_mrn`, `nurse_id`, `status` (e.g., "Synced", "Pending", "Local Only"), and `source_system` fields. Audit events include `action`, `user_id`, `timestamp`, `ip_address`, and `details`, and are retained for 7 years. All tables are encrypted at rest using Azure-managed keys, and we’ll use row-level security to restrict access by nurse and ward.

Thanks, the stored entities and their fields are recorded. The shift roster stays out of the database, which keeps the 90-second roster drop tied to the ward shift system.

Retention is the gap now. Patient notes need a retention period separate from the audit trail. Default: patient notes kept for 7 years, matching the audit retention, then archived under the hospital's records policy. Keep this default?

Yes, we’ll keep the default: patient notes are retained in Azure SQL for 7 years, aligned with our hospital’s medical records retention policy and HIPAA requirements. After 7 years, they are automatically archived to a secure, immutable blob container in Azure with a 10-year retention period, and the archive is tagged with a `retention_status = archived` flag. The system does not delete notes during the 7-year window, and the charge nurse dashboard shows a warning when a note approaches its retention end. This ensures compliance with both legal and clinical governance standards.

Retention for patient notes is recorded as 7 years in Azure SQL, then archived to immutable blob storage for 10 more years.

One question on the data relationships. When a nurse edits a note offline and it conflicts with an Epic version, should the app keep every version as its own record linked to the note, or overwrite the local record with the latest one by timestamp? Default: keep every version linked to the note, so nothing is lost in an audit.

Version history is recorded: every version of an edited note is kept and linked to the note.

Finding f45-1: the roster_load_time metric has no defined measurement method or threshold, so the 3-second roster load requirement can't be tested yet. Default: roster_load_time is the time from the roster request to the full roster being displayed, with a 3-second threshold. That means the metric is captured in Application Insights for every sign-in and a test fails if the median is above 3 seconds. Keep this default?

Yes, we’ll keep the default: `roster_load_time` is measured from the moment the nurse clicks “Load Roster” to the moment the last patient card is rendered on screen, captured via client-side JavaScript timing and logged in Azure Application Insights. The test fails if the 90th percentile of load times exceeds 3 seconds over a 5-minute rolling window. This ensures consistent performance across devices and network conditions, and aligns with our user experience SLA.

Thanks, the roster_load_time definition is recorded: measured from "Load Roster" to the last card rendered, with a 90th-percentile threshold of 3 seconds over a 5-minute window.

Staying on data: when a note is queued locally and later synced, how long should the app keep the local copy of the note on the device? Default: until the server confirms the sync, then remove it from the device so no patient data stays on the tablet.

Yes, we’ll keep the default: the app retains the local copy of the note on the device only until the .NET backend confirms successful sync to Epic via the FHIR API. Once confirmed, the note is deleted from IndexedDB and the local cache. This ensures no patient data remains on the device after sync, minimizing risk if a tablet is lost or stolen. summary:
The system will run on Azure, integrating with Azure AD for SSO and Azure AD B2C for external access. It connects to Epic via FHIR API (STU3) for patient data and a ward-level nurse scheduling system via REST API for real-time staffing, all proxied through Azure API Management for HIPAA compliance. The in-house team consists of two full-stack developers, one React frontend specialist, and one DevOps engineer, using Azure DevOps, Terraform, SonarQube, and Snyk.

The tool addresses clinical note duplication, causing 3–5 minute delays per patient per shift and an 18% error rate. Primary users are ward nurses managing 12–15 patients per shift, with secondary users being charge nurses, tertiary users being clinical informatics leads, and pharmacy liaisons with read-only access for specific alerts. The stack is .NET and C#.

Version one must be live by October 15, 2024, to align with the hospital’s compliance audit and EMR upgrade. It will include core note entry, FHIR push to Epic, and a basic dashboard for charge nurses, with PDF as the only export format. The budget is $85,000, covering in-house development, Azure infrastructure, API management, and compliance testing, with a commercial FHIR client library (Hl7.FhirNetCore) and licensed logging/monitoring tools.

After SSO login, ward nurses see a dashboard listing their shift patients. They click a patient card to open a pre-filled note form, type a free-text note with auto-save every 30 seconds, select a note type, and submit. The note is sent to Epic via FHIR API and appears in the charge nurse dashboard. Hospital IT administrators monitor the tool via Azure Monitor and Application Insights. If Epic is unreachable during submission, the note is immediately persisted to our Azure SQL Database with a status of “Pending” and a retry queue is triggered via Azure Service Bus. The system automatically retries the FHIR POST every 30 seconds for up to 15 minutes, with exponential backoff. If it fails after 15 minutes, the nurse receives a notification in-app: “Note saved locally—sync failed. Contact IT if issue persists.” The charge nurse dashboard also flags pending notes by red icon, and the IT admin sees retry failures in Azure Monitor. This ensures no data loss and keeps nurses productive during transient outages.

At launch, about 160 active ward nurses will use the tool, with peak concurrency of 60–80 users during shifts and up to 120 during shift changes. Azure App Service will be provisioned with 4 vCPUs, scaling to 8 instances during peak times.

The system enforces HIPAA compliance and the hospital’s internal data governance policy, including mandatory encryption at rest and in transit (using Azure’s managed keys and TLS 1.3), audit logging for all access and modifications (retained for 7 years), and strict role-based access control via Azure AD. All FHIR data transfers are subject to the audit trail policy, and Microsoft Purview is enabled for data classification and discovery. Data residency is limited to the U.S. region (Azure East US), with encrypted backups stored in a separate region for disaster recovery.

The pharmacy liaison sees only alert-flagged notes. When a nurse submits a note with the alert type “Patient refusing medication,” the system tags it in Azure SQL with a `priority_flag = true` and sets `alert_type = "refusal"`. The pharmacy liaison, viewing the curated dashboard, sees a red banner notification highlighting the note, with the patient’s name, MRN, bed number, time of note, and the full text. They can click to open it, which triggers an automated workflow: a Microsoft Teams message is sent to the pharmacy team channel with a link to the note, and a ticket is created in ServiceNow with priority level 2. The liaison does not edit or delete the note—only reviews and escalates. Only the pharmacy liaison and the charge nurse can open an alert-flagged note, and each access is logged in Azure Monitor with the user ID, timestamp, IP address, and the note’s MRN. When the liaison opens the note, they must select a reason from a dropdown—“Initiate intervention,” “Review for clinical risk,” or “Confirm no action”—which is stored in the audit log and visible in the data governance portal. This ensures accountability and supports the 7-year audit retention policy. No other role may access alert notes directly.

At the end of their shift, the ward nurse can access a “Shift Summary” view that shows all notes they submitted during the shift, with color-coded status: green for “Synced to Epic,” yellow for “Pending retry,” and red for “Failed after 15 minutes.” They can tap any failed note to see the error message and retry it manually if desired. The system also highlights any notes they flagged as “urgent” or “alert” so they can confirm handoffs were properly escalated. This summary is auto-saved and available in the app for 24 hours after shift end, and can be exported to PDF for personal records.

The Epic contract is FHIR STU3 with OAuth 2.0 client credentials through Azure API Management, with errors mapped to the retry rules.

At the start of their shift, the charge nurse opens the dashboard and sees a real-time summary of all ward notes from the prior shift: a list of patients with active notes, color-coded by status—green for “synced,” yellow for “pending,” and red for “failed.” They immediately see any alert-flagged notes (e.g., “refusing medication”) in a dedicated section at the top with a red badge, and a count of unresolved issues. They can click “View Full Log” to drill into the full note history per patient or export the overview to PDF for handoff. The system auto-refreshes every 2 minutes during the shift.

The PDF handoff is shared with the incoming charge nurse and the unit manager, who receive it via secure email through Azure Logic Apps, with encryption and a 7-day expiration link. The export is logged in the audit trail with the user ID, timestamp, patient count, and recipient email, and stored in Azure Blob Storage with a 7-year retention policy—exactly like alert-note access. This ensures compliance with HIPAA and the internal data governance policy, and allows tracing any data sharing during audits.

While waiting to retry, the nurse sees a persistent notification at the top of the screen: “Your note is pending sync—will retry automatically. Status: Retry attempt #2 (30 seconds ago).” The retry status updates every 30 seconds with a progress graphic. If the note fails after 15 minutes, the system triggers a push notification (via Azure Notification Hub) and displays a modal: “Note saved locally—sync failed due to Epic outage. Contact IT if issue persists.” The message remains visible until acknowledged, ensuring no note is silently lost—this is logged as a failed write event in Azure Monitor, visible to the IT team.

When a nurse opens the app, they must authenticate via Azure AD SSO and immediately see their assigned shift roster—displayed as a list of patient cards—with real-time status indicators (e.g., “Active,” “Discharged,” “Transfer”). The ward shift system follows the same integration pattern as Epic: REST on Azure behind API Management, with OAuth 2.0 client credentials and the same error-mapping approach. ## Product overview and problem

### Overview

Ward nurses currently enter clinical notes twice: once into Epic’s FHIR note field and once into a shared Excel ward log. This duplication consumes 3 to 5 minutes per patient per shift, leads to an 18% error rate, and creates compliance risks. The product will unify note entry into a single system that pushes notes automatically to Epic and maintains a ward log dashboard. It will reduce duplication, errors, and compliance risk.

The tool must be live by October 15, 2024, built in-house on an $85,000 budget, using Azure cloud infrastructure, licensed FHIR libraries, and monitoring tools.

## Business rules

### Business Rules

- Notes for patients marked as Transferred or Discharged in the ward shift system must be locally saved only unless reviewed.
- Nurses can submit notes to Epic only for patients assigned to their ward.
- Patient status from the ward shift system takes precedence over Epic data.
- Transferred patients’ notes may be submitted to Epic with auditing and flags.
- Local-only saved notes purge after 7 days unless manually reviewed.
- Charge nurse and clinical informatics lead may release local-only notes to Epic or mark reviewed.
- Patient cards for transferred patients must be removed within 90 seconds of status update.

These rules ensure data integrity, compliance, and prevent invalid submissions.

## Technical requirements

### Technical Requirements

- Hosting: Azure Cloud (existing infrastructure compatibility).
- Backend: .NET / C# leveraging Azure App Services with scaling.
- Frontend: React with TypeScript (Create React App).
- FHIR integration: Hl7.FhirNetCore commercial library.
- Authentication and Authorization: Azure AD SSO with roles, OAuth 2.0 client credentials for API access.
- Deployment and CI/CD: Azure DevOps pipelines with Terraform.
- Static code quality tools: SonarQube and Snyk.
- Offline note support via IndexedDB and service workers with conflict resolution.
- Secure hosting of frontend and backend with HTTPS and protections against CSP and XSS.

These choices support security, maintainability, HIPAA compliance, and performance under peak loads.

## Data requirements

### Data Requirements

- Entities:
  - **Notes:** include created_at, updated_at, patient_mrn, nurse_id, status, source_system; linked to audit_events.
  - **Audit Events:** record actions with user_id, timestamp, IP, and details.
- Note retention: Patient notes stored for 7 years in Azure SQL, then archived immutably for 10 years.
- Local device copies saved in IndexedDB are deleted after confirmation of Epic sync; failed notes queued for manual retry.
- All note versions preserved, including conflicting offline edits.

These data requirements ensure full auditability and compliance.

## Integrations

### Integrations

- Epic EMR via FHIR STU3 API for reading patient demographics and admission status and writing notes.
- Ward Shift System via REST API for real-time ward staffing and validation.
- Both accessed via Azure API Management with OAuth 2.0 client credentials.
- The API contract for Epic is defined as FHIR STU3 to provide a stable interface before integration.

These integrations enable accurate, timely patient and shift data and secure note submission.

## Security and privacy

### Security and Privacy

- Compliance with HIPAA and hospital data governance.
- Encryption at rest and in transit using Azure managed keys and TLS 1.3.
- Audit logging of all access and edits, retained for 7 years.
- Data residency limited to Azure East US region.
- Access control via Azure AD roles with MFA.
- Pharmacy liaison access strictly read-only, requires explicit approval and audit logging.
- Role definitions and membership managed via Azure AD groups, revoked upon staff changes.

These measures protect patient data and meet regulatory requirements.

## Non-functional requirements

### Non-Functional Requirements

- Support approximately 160 nurses at launch.
- System must handle 60–80 concurrent editors at peak, up to 120 sessions at shift change.
- Backend hosted on Azure App Service with 4 vCPU, autoscaling to 8 instances based on CPU and request queue length.
- Frontend and backend must meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards.

These ensure performance, scalability, and usability.

## Administrative surface

### Administrative Surface

- Health monitoring dashboard accessible to Hospital IT administrators, showing API latency, error rates, authentication failures.
- Secure admin portal for clinical informatics lead to audit note distribution and duplication.
- Audit logs and reports stored and accessible as required.

No other administrative interfaces are planned at launch.

Version one includes core note entry by ward nurses, push of notes to Epic via FHIR, and basic charge nurse dashboard with PDF export of summaries.
